#5459. From Working the Drive-Thru at Wendy’s to Becoming the CEO of EBONY — Eden Bridgeman Shares the Lessons That Built Her Leadership Style

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

EBONY CEO Eden Bridgeman explains how her franchise background and her father’s leadership lessons are helping her take an 80-year-old cultural institution into the future of media.

Eden Bridgeman began her working life with shifts at Wendy’s and Chili’s—jobs that taught her key lessons on a career path that put her in the driver’s seat of one of the most iconic brands in media history.

Bridgeman went on from working behind the counter to becoming the CMO of Manna, Inc., a restaurant franchise operator. And in 2021, after her father, the late Ulysses “Junior” Bridgeman, bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020, she took the reins of EBONY.

This fall, EBONY unveiled its 2026 Power 100 list, a class that stretches from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator, all celebrated at a gala at the Hollywood Palladium under the theme “The Stories We Shape.” One of the categories, the Junior Bridgeman Business Vanguard, is named in her father’s honor.

Following the event, Bridgeman shared her thoughts on leadership that serves your team, finding success in the attention economy and defining power that truly makes an impact.

As a teenager, you worked at Wendy’s and Chili’s. What is one specific habit or rule from those shifts that you still use as a CEO? One thing I learned very early is that the customer experiences the whole business, not your department. If something was wrong with an order, the customer did not care whether the mistake happened at the register, in the kitchen, or somewhere else. They simply knew the experience did not meet their expectations. Working in restaurants teaches you very quickly that everyone has some responsibility for the final outcome. Restaurants also taught me the importance of staying close to the business. You learn things from the front line that you cannot always see in a report.

You were CMO of a restaurant franchise operator, and then took over an 80-year old media brand. What surprised you most about the media business? Honestly, how many businesses exist inside of the media business. Coming from restaurants, there were certainly complexities, but the economic model was relatively clear. Media has a very different ecosystem. You have the audience consuming the product, advertisers funding parts of the business, platforms influencing distribution, creators and talent shaping relevance, technology affecting discovery, and increasingly commerce and experiences creating additional revenue opportunities. All of those constituencies matter, but they do not always want the same thing.

That requires a different kind of discipline. One of the biggest lessons for me has been that attention and revenue are not the same thing. A piece of content can perform extremely well culturally and still not create meaningful business value unless you have built the right infrastructure around that attention.

What practices from the restaurant world do you think can apply to success in media? There are actually quite a few. The first is frequency. Restaurants understand that growth is not just about convincing somebody to visit once. The second is consistency. In restaurants, brand standards exist because people expect a certain experience every time they walk through the door. Media brands need that same clarity. And then there is measurement. Restaurant businesses are incredibly disciplined about understanding performance at a granular level. You know what is selling, when it is selling and where there are operational problems. I bring that mindset to EBONY because I believe creativity becomes more powerful when you understand its impact.

Your father bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020. When you took over in 2021, what were the first things you fixed or rebuilt? I tend to be careful with the word “fixed,” because it can suggest that everything before you was wrong. That is not how I view EBONY. We inherited an extraordinary brand with generations of cultural equity, but the business around that brand had to operate in a fundamentally different media environment. So much of my focus has been on rebuilding the infrastructure necessary for EBONY to compete as a modern media company. That means strengthening how we operate, how we sell, how we develop partnerships, how we think about content and distribution, and how we measure whether the work is producing the outcomes we intended.

But there was also a more philosophical question that had to be answered: What does it mean to modernize EBONY without disconnecting it from what made it important in the first place? There are generations of people who have a personal relationship with this brand. Then there is a younger generation whose relationship with media, culture and identity is completely different. My responsibility is not to choose between those audiences. It is to understand the fundamental truth that made EBONY matter historically and translate that truth into products, experiences and storytelling that feel relevant now. Legacy gives you permission to enter the conversation. Relevance determines whether people continue listening.

Are there any leadership lessons or words of encouragement from your father that you think about regularly? I would describe it less as one particular quote and more as a leadership philosophy I learned from my father: the inverted pyramid.

The idea is that leadership is not about positioning yourself at the top with everyone working up toward you. You turn the pyramid upside down. As a leader, your responsibility is to support the people doing the work and make sure they have what they need to be successful.

That has stayed with me because it changes the way you think about leadership. A title may give you authority, but leadership is really about service, accountability and creating the conditions for other people to succeed.

As CEO, I try to remember that my role is not to have every answer or to be the center of every decision. My responsibility is to provide clarity around where we are going, remove obstacles where I can, make the difficult decisions when necessary, and give the team the support and accountability they need to do their best work.

I think that philosophy takes on another layer at EBONY. There is a responsibility to the people working to move the business forward, but also to the audience and community that have trusted this brand for generations.

The higher you move in an organization, the more people you are responsible for serving, not the more people who are responsible for serving you.

My father led humbly, as a servant leader, and that is the lesson from him I carry most directly into how I try to lead today.

Where do you think are the biggest opportunities for EBONY and other legacy media brands in today’s media landscape? I think the biggest opportunity is to stop defining a media company primarily by the content it publishes. Content will always be essential, but it can extend into original intellectual property, experiences, commerce, recommendations, partnerships and new forms of distribution. It can create opportunities for brands that want genuine cultural credibility. And it gives us the ability to convene communities both digitally and physically.

I also believe there is significant opportunity in understanding audiences more deeply. Our history is an enormous competitive advantage, but history cannot become an excuse for standing still. Younger consumers are not obligated to love EBONY because their parents or grandparents did. We have to earn their relationship with the brand on their terms.

If we can combine the trust and cultural authority built over generations with the technology, formats, distribution and business models available today, I think the opportunity is much larger than traditional publishing.

The Power 100 honorees range from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator. How do you define “power”?

I think power has become much more distributed. Traditionally, we tended to associate power with institutions: the person running the company, controlling capital, holding political office or deciding who gained access. Those forms of power still matter enormously. But technology and social platforms have created entirely different ways for people to build influence.

A young person can create something from their bedroom and develop an audience larger than many traditional media outlets. A creator can introduce millions of people to an idea, product or cause almost instantly. An entrepreneur can build a community without first receiving permission from a traditional gatekeeper.

That changes the way we should think about power. For EBONY, I think power is ultimately about the ability to create meaningful impact. Can you shift a conversation? Can you open a door that was previously closed? Can you build something that creates opportunity for other people? Can you influence how people see themselves or what they believe is possible? When I think about power today, I am interested not only in who has it, but what they are doing with it.

Eden Bridgeman began her working life with shifts at Wendy’s and Chili’s—jobs that taught her key lessons on a career path that put her in the driver’s seat of one of the most iconic brands in media history.

Bridgeman went on from working behind the counter to becoming the CMO of Manna, Inc., a restaurant franchise operator. And in 2021, after her father, the late Ulysses “Junior” Bridgeman, bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020, she took the reins of EBONY.

This fall, EBONY unveiled its 2026 Power 100 list, a class that stretches from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator, all celebrated at a gala at the Hollywood Palladium under the theme “The Stories We Shape.” One of the categories, the Junior Bridgeman Business Vanguard, is named in her father’s honor.

#5458. Nvidia abruptly changed how it reported revenue in Singapore last year, adding to questions about its relationship with Megaspeed

A sudden change in how Nvidia reported some of its financial results last year is getting renewed attention, raising questions about its relationship with Megaspeed, a major Nvidia client at the time and now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

The financial change under scrutiny involves Nvidia’s accounting for revenue from Singapore, where Megaspeed is based.

Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of the semiconductor chip giant on Thursday, following stunning revelations of his affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation), a woman suspected of being an operative for China. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress will lead the company in the interim, Nvidia announced on Thursday.

Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Asia, has been suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, in violation of U.S. export laws. Megaspeed, and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric, moved at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China, tech news site The Information has reported.

Singapore authorities said on Thursday that they investigated Megaspeed and its former executive Alice Huang beginning in February 2025 and did not find sufficient evidence of espionage. However, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country. The U.S. is also investigating Megaspeed for export control violations. Jensen Huang has previously said there is no evidence of Nvidia chips being smuggled to China, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

In June 2025, Nvidia added Megaspeed to its internal block list, prohibiting sales to the company, according to the Wall Street Journal. Around the same time, Nvidia stopped reporting revenue from Singapore, one of the five geographic areas Nvidia had previously listed in its breakdown of global revenues (they were U.S., Singapore, Taiwan, China, and “Other”).

In the fiscal quarter ending in July 2025, Nvidia reported $10.2 billion in revenue from Singapore, 22% of the company’s total revenue, and an 81% increase in year-over-year revenue from the country. In the next quarter’s earnings report, for the three months ending in October 2025, Singapore had disappeared from Nvidia’s geographic revenue breakdown, which now listed only four markets: U.S., Taiwan, China, and Other.

According to the October 2025 earnings report, Nvidia was now separating out markets based on “location of the customers’ headquarters” instead of “customer billing location.” The change was made even though Nvidia’s previous earnings reports had clearly stated that “customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere.”

Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment, including an inquiry if the change in how it reported its earnings was at all connected to it adding Megaspeed to its block list.

Shiva Rajgopal, a professor of accounting and auditing at Columbia Business School, told Fortune correlation is not causation, and it is impossible to say with just public information whether concerns around Megaspeed’s export control adherence or Alice Huang’s alleged espionage caused Nvidia to change how it reported revenue. However, he noted, Nvidia’s changes in the filings will no doubt become part of the Department of Justice or Department of Commerce’s investigations into Nvidia’s export control compliance.

“The timing is curious,” Rajgopal said. “Even if it is not curious, people are going to raise questions given all this information now.”

Auditors will likely look at what Nvidia knew about where the Megaspeed chips were ending up, how Nvidia checked and documented customer end-use, and if Huang’s affair was related to Nvidia’s business with Megaspeed. But they will also look at whether investors were given an accurate picture of the risks associated with potential smuggling in China and Southeast Asia. Rajgopal made it clear that as CFO, Kress’ role in how finances were disclosed publicly, will certainly be scrutinized, but based on public filings alone, there does not appear to be evidence at this time showing Kress was aware of whether an earnings reporting change could have potentially been related to Megaspeed.

“I wouldn’t say Kress must have known,” Rajgopal said. “These are just financial statements. Nothing is illegal. It’s disclosed.”

Rajgopal argued Kress’s biggest challenge has little to do with the company’s past or immediate finances. Finance executives who take interim chief executive roles in tech companies rarely stay because they lack the buy-in of the tech community, he said. Nvidia’s priorities will soon shift from sustaining its financial momentum today to working to recreate or build upon the forward vision Huang gave the company, which is a decidedly different role than a finance head.

“A CFO running a tech company is not a good idea,” Rajgopal said, “especially something that’s so deeply tech-heavy.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5457. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

#5456. 3 Ways Businesses Can Create Lasting Value Across Borders

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From building relationships to adapting to local markets, lasting growth depends on more than simply expanding a company’s reach.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Asia has undergone an extraordinary economic transformation over the past several decades. Countries that once played relatively modest roles in international commerce have become important centers of manufacturing, technology, finance and innovation.

What interests me most about this transformation is not simply the speed of growth, but the way businesses across the region have learned to operate in markets with very different cultures, languages and economic conditions.

Consider Southeast Asia. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment into the region reached $226 billion in 2024, an increase of 8% even as global investment flows declined. The region has become an important part of international supply chains, connecting businesses and customers across Asia and beyond.

Yet Asia is not a single market. Doing business in Singapore is very different from doing business in Vietnam, Indonesia or Japan. Each has its own expectations, regulations and ways of building relationships.

I believe this diversity is precisely what makes Asia such an interesting place from which to learn. For entrepreneurs looking to expand internationally, three lessons stand out.

In many parts of Asia, business relationships are built gradually. People want to understand who they are dealing with, whether they can rely on them and whether there is a genuine commitment to working together.

This is not unique to Asia, of course, but it is particularly relevant in a region where business practices and cultural expectations can vary considerably between countries.

When entering a new market, entrepreneurs naturally focus on commercial opportunities. They study demand, calculate potential returns and consider how quickly they can establish operations. These are important questions, but they should not come at the expense of understanding people.

The Asian Development Bank’s Asian Economic Integration Report 2025 examines how regional cooperation, investment and participation in global value chains have helped shape Asia’s economic development.

Behind these economic relationships are businesses that must learn to work together across borders. Reliable partnerships, mutual understanding and the ability to resolve differences are essential to making that cooperation successful.

I have always believed that trust is built through consistency. People remember whether we honor our commitments, communicate honestly and treat them fairly when difficulties arise.

A partnership may begin with a commercial agreement, but its strength is often tested when circumstances change. Markets can become uncertain, costs can rise, and plans do not always unfold as expected.

For entrepreneurs, the lesson is to resist the temptation to treat relationships simply as a means of entering a market. Take time to understand local expectations, listen carefully and choose partners whose values are compatible with your own.

The strongest relationships are often those that continue long after the first transaction has been completed.

One of the most valuable lessons from Asia is that geographical proximity does not necessarily mean cultural or commercial similarity.

A business that succeeds in Singapore cannot assume that the same approach will work in Thailand or Indonesia. Consumer preferences, purchasing habits, regulations and expectations of service can differ significantly. This makes Asia an excellent reminder that international expansion requires flexibility.

The OECD’s 2026 Digital Trade Review of ASEAN highlights both the region’s growing digital opportunities and the regulatory differences that continue to complicate cross-border business.

The report estimates that ASEAN’s digital trade exports have reached $387 billion, representing nearly 20% of the region’s total exports. At the same time, differences in national regulations and cross-border data requirements remain obstacles to deeper integration.

For businesses, the implications are clear. Technology may make it easier to reach customers in another country, but it does not eliminate the need to understand how that market operates.

I believe successful international businesses distinguish between the principles they should preserve and the practices they should be willing to change.

A company’s commitment to quality, integrity and customer service should remain consistent wherever it operates. But how those commitments are delivered may need to be adapted to local circumstances.

This requires listening to local employees and customers rather than assuming that decisions made at headquarters will always be appropriate. It also requires humility. Entrepreneurs need confidence in their ideas, but they must remain willing to acknowledge when something is not working.

Sometimes the wisest decision is to test a smaller opportunity, learn from the response and adjust before committing substantial resources.

Asia’s diversity reminds us that successful expansion is not about imposing the same formula everywhere. It is about understanding what people value and finding a way to meet their needs without compromising what the business stands for.

Perhaps the most important lesson from Asia’s economic development is the value of investing in people, skills and long-term capabilities.

Many of the region’s economies have developed through participation in international production networks. Businesses do not necessarily manufacture an entire product in one country. Instead, different stages of production take place across several markets, drawing on specialized skills and resources.

The ASEAN Investment Report 2025 highlights how investment has supported the development of regional supply chains in industries including semiconductors, automotive manufacturing and apparel.

This is significant because international investment can contribute more than capital. When supported by training, knowledge-sharing and strong local partnerships, it can help businesses and workers develop capabilities that remain valuable over time.

For entrepreneurs, I believe there is an important distinction between establishing operations in another country and becoming a meaningful part of its economy.

A business may open an office, hire employees and begin generating revenue. But if every important decision is made elsewhere and local people have few opportunities to develop, its long-term contribution may be limited.

By contrast, businesses that invest in training, develop local leaders and encourage the exchange of knowledge can create stronger foundations for growth.

This does not require a large organization or an elaborate program. Smaller businesses can provide mentoring, professional development and opportunities for employees to take on greater responsibility.

These investments may not deliver immediate financial returns, but they help build the experience and confidence that organizations need as they grow.

I also believe there is something important about creating opportunities that extend beyond the business itself. When people acquire new skills, they carry that knowledge throughout their careers. Their development can benefit other organizations, industries and communities.

Asia’s experience demonstrates the potential of economies working together while developing their own capabilities. Entrepreneurs everywhere can learn from that approach.

Asia’s economic success has not followed a single model. Different countries have developed their own strengths, and the region continues to face challenges involving trade, regulation and economic uncertainty. Nevertheless, its experience offers useful lessons for businesses seeking opportunities beyond their home markets.

Relationships require patience. Local differences deserve respect. And lasting growth depends on developing people and capabilities, not simply increasing sales.

There will always be pressure to expand quickly, particularly when competitors appear to be moving ahead. But entering more markets is not necessarily the same as building a stronger business.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to consider not only where their next opportunity might be, but also what they can contribute when they get there. Can they become trusted partners? Can they serve customers in ways that reflect local needs? Can they create opportunities for people to learn and grow?

These questions may not produce the fastest route to expansion, but they encourage a more sustainable approach to international business.

To me, the greatest lesson from Asia is that creating value across borders requires more than the movement of goods, services and capital. It requires an understanding of people and a willingness to build relationships that endure.

Businesses that recognize this have an opportunity to achieve something more meaningful than international reach. They can create lasting value wherever they operate.

Asia has undergone an extraordinary economic transformation over the past several decades. Countries that once played relatively modest roles in international commerce have become important centers of manufacturing, technology, finance and innovation.

What interests me most about this transformation is not simply the speed of growth, but the way businesses across the region have learned to operate in markets with very different cultures, languages and economic conditions.

Consider Southeast Asia. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment into the region reached $226 billion in 2024, an increase of 8% even as global investment flows declined. The region has become an important part of international supply chains, connecting businesses and customers across Asia and beyond.

#5455. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5454. A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.

Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off.

In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period.

The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting. Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday. LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress.

Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s.

The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together.

In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself.

NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners.

Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties. Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited.

In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik, president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor.

LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency in both Sag Harbor and Manhattan.

Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote, defeating Lukas Ventouras, a 25-year-old law student and district resident who had raised about $124,000, mostly in unitemized small-dollar donations. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise. LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate.

Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies, a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.”

He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district.

LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune. “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times, he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.”

Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations.

LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand.

The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 16% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle.

Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 totaling nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million.

Half of that in-district money, about $159,000, came from the Hamptons and Shelter Island, the East End enclaves where wealthy New Yorkers have long kept second homes. In East Hampton Town, half of the 22,562 housing units are no one’s usual residence, according to the Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 American Community Survey, which counts second homes as vacant. In Brookhaven, the figure is only about 9%.

Outside the district, 218 Manhattan donors gave Gallant $215,600 and 85 Californians gave about $93,000. Thirteen listed San Francisco.

The photos worked as a fundraiser, just not a local one. Between Sept. 13 and Oct. 14, Gallant reported 677 itemized contributions totaling $276,055: $229,050 from 484 individual donors and $47,005 from PACs, party committees and other sources.

That haul, all in the campaign’s final month of reporting, is about 16% of the $1.7 million he raised this cycle and nearly a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals in 2026. About a third of it arrived in the first four days after the leak.

On Sept. 15, two days after the leak, the New York State Democratic Committee transferred $25,025 to the campaign. That same day, the campaign paid Sara Azari, the celebrity attorney who specializes in crisis and media strategy.

Among the contributions that followed: $500 on Sept. 15 from Howard Sacarob, head of U.S. Tax at Royal Bank of Canada, and $3,500 on Oct. 4 from Ryan Fitzpatrick, Corcoran’s regional vice president for Downtown Manhattan.

On Oct. 7, the New York Times published its own analysis of the photo scandal. That day, Robert Saum, the World Bank Group’s regional country director for Eastern Europe, a role based in Kyiv, gave $1,000. He lists an Arlington, Va., address.

Steven Holley, COO of the New York investment manager Select Equity Group and former Sullivan & Cromwell partner, gave $1,000 on Oct. 9. Sacarob, Fitzpatrick and Holley all list New York City addresses, outside the district.

The San Francisco-based CEO of Mr. S Leather, the retailer behind the photos, gave $1,000 on Oct. 10.

Not all of Gallant’s best-known donors gave after the Post story. Fortune checked the names below against the dates in his filings.

Wall Street: Stephen Mandel, who founded the Greenwich hedge fund Lone Pine Capital, gave the $3,500 maximum on Sept. 14, the day after the story ran. Susan Mandel of Greenwich, listed as not employed, gave $3,500 the same day.

Old money and real estate: Katharine Rayner, the Cox Enterprises heiress whose fortune of about $4.9 billion (Forbes) rests on her estimated 17% stake in the family company, gave $3,500 on Sept. 15. She had also given $2,000 in July, and her cycle total is listed at the $3,500 limit.

Another maximum gift came on Sept. 26 from Michael Raynes, a developer who restores architecturally significant properties in Miami. In late 2022, he sold a historic estate in Southampton for $20 million. He lists a Miami Beach mailing address.

Wall Street: Charles Myers gave the $3,500 maximum at the end of 2025, when Gallant was still facing a primary. He is founder and chairman of Signum Global Advisors, a geopolitical research firm that advises financial institutions and touts “representation across the political spectrum.” He previously served as vice chairman at Evercore ISI and advised Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign.

Jason Carroll, co-founder of the high-frequency trading firm Hudson River Trading, gave $3,500 on Sept. 8, five days before the leak. Eric Knight, a senior trader at Jane Street, gave $7,000, covering both the primary and the general.

Hollywood and media: Kevin Huvane, co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency, gave $3,500 on June 30. Jeffrey Bewkes, the former Time Warner chairman and CEO who sold the company to AT&T in 2018, gave $3,500 on Aug. 12.

Local: Nancy Goroff, an organic chemist and former chair of Stony Brook University’s chemistry department, gave the maximum on June 29, days after Gallant’s primary win. Goroff lives in a modest New England saltbox overlooking Stony Brook Harbor, valued at about $1.1 million. She ran for a similarly drawn seat in 2020, losing to Lee Zeldin, now President Trump’s EPA administrator.

Goroff also backed “Team KCQ,” North Fork educator Kathryn Casey Quigley’s progressive bid to oust Suffolk County Democratic Chairman Rich Schaffer. Casey Quigley won about 43% of the weighted county committee vote on Sept. 22. Her campaign accused Schaffer of “backroom deals” with the local Conservative Party, which had harshly condemned Gallant’s photos.

Wall Street: Charles Schwab, founder of the brokerage bearing his name, a Fortune 500 company, gave LaLota $13,600 over the past two cycles, the maximum allowed. His mailing city: Palm Beach, Fla.

Crypto and defense: Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer and a deputy national security adviser under George W. Bush, gave $3,500 from a Washington, D.C., address. Palmer Luckey of Newport Beach, Calif., who founded defense contractor Anduril after selling Oculus to Facebook for about $2 billion, gave $7,000.

Global money: Leonard Blavatnik, the Ukrainian-born British American billionaire (Forbes) behind Access Industries, gave LaLota $3,500 in March. FEC reports list another $7,000 in aggregate from his wife, Emily.

“Though I have never met him, I appreciate his support,” LaLota said. His spokeswoman suggested Blavatnik may be drawn to LaLota because Russia’s Foreign Ministry put LaLota on a May 2023 list of 500 Americans barred from the country, a distinction the congressman “wears as a badge of honor.”

Blavatnik’s recent contributions also include Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and the Equality PAC, which backs LGBTQ+ candidates.

His contribution forms give an address of 40 W. 57th St. in Manhattan, about 105 miles from the estate the press calls his.

The July 2025 sale of 408 Further Lane in Amagansett, which Behind the Hedges reported as the most expensive residential sale in Hamptons history, lists Brise Lointaine LLC as the new owner.

The seller, Terry Semel, ran Warner Bros. when Stanley Kubrick filmed his masked Long Island society for the studio. Semel had bought the property from Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman in 2005 for $43 million.

Property records from the real estate data service PropertyShark, reviewed by Fortune, list the arm’s-length price as $115,000, three zeros shy of the reported $115 million. East Hampton’s 2026 tax roll still billed Semel’s Windsor Digital Studio LLC. The town assessor’s office said it did not update the roll until July 2026.

The East Hampton Town Clerk’s office confirmed Brise Lointaine LLC’s ownership to Fortune and said deed updates take “very long” to process, along with the Suffolk County Clerk’s office.

Press accounts, though not the paperwork, identify the buyer as LaLota donor Len Blavatnik: Behind the Hedges, citing a source, and The Real Deal. Blavatnik owns Warner Music and holds a stake in A24, the arthouse studio behind Lady Bird (2017), Queer (2024), the gay BDSM romance Pillion (2026) and Backrooms (2026).

The tabloid framing of the race borrowed from Eyes Wide Shut (1999), but the sex and the masks were bait. Kubrick’s real horror was a gated order where wealth and power circulate in a closed circle, insulated from consequences.

In his year, the guest list was paper: electronic filing stayed voluntary for most committees until 2000, so a donor was a scanned page, not a spreadsheet. In NY-1, the circle is no secret.

In an age of metadata, AI-scanned social feeds and Flock cameras, nobody wears a mask for long. The leather shoot was archived, authenticated by an attorney and sold back to voters as merchandise. Every FEC filing is a digital fossil Kubrick’s guests would never have left behind.

The economics were another matter. LaLota raised about 84 cents of every named dollar from outside the district; Gallant, nearly two-thirds. What stayed masked on Election Day was not Gallant’s leather photos but the money, and how much of it came from outside NY-1.

#5453. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:09 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”

#5452. Small Business Owners Have More AI Insight Than Ever — But It’s Stuck in Dashboards. Here’s How to Put It to Work.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Small business owners today have access to a significant volume of data when it comes to managing their business, and their employee data may reveal insights that are hiding in plain sight.  Most business leaders have access to workforce dashboards to track turnover, overtime, engagement, cost per hire in real time, and more. What they truly need is the ability to turn that data into a decision before the moment that matters has passed.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Small business owners have access to more workforce data than ever, and that data may hold insights hiding in plain sight. Most business leaders can track turnover, overtime, engagement, cost per hire and more on real-time dashboards. What they really need is the ability to turn that data into a decision before the moment that matters has passed.

That gap was highlighted in Paychex’s 2026 Business Leaders Priorities Report, which found that AI adoption and usage rank among the top challenges keeping businesses tied to slower, costlier processes. Many people assume the barrier is a lack of information. In reality, most small businesses already have plenty of workforce data and plenty of tools telling them what it means. The real barrier is speed and, increasingly, proof.

HR leaders are now expected to justify workforce decisions to the C-suite as they happen, not just at the end of a quarter. Decisions are often made before a meeting ends. Leaders need a clear view of their workforce, including why a staffing or scheduling decision was made, before the change shows up on a P&L.

This is becoming a major pressure point for many small businesses, and it’s exposing a design flaw that has existed in workforce technology for years: Insight and action live in different places.

A dashboard can tell a business leader that something needs attention, but acting on it often means switching to another system. Every extra step gives the moment a chance to pass. By the time a decision is made, it’s reactive instead of strategic, and the leader defending it has to reconstruct the reasoning after the fact instead of pointing to it in the moment.

Consider a restaurant owner whose overtime costs are trending above budget. A dashboard might flag the issue, but if that insight only appears in a report reviewed days later, the costs may already be locked in. When the same insight surfaces in the scheduling system the owner or manager uses every day, they can review staffing levels and adjust sooner, before the trend becomes a bigger problem that takes longer to fix.

When workforce insight sits in a separate report or standalone dashboard, it competes with everything else on a leader’s plate that day. It’s one more tab, one more login, one more thing to remember to check. If a busy owner or manager doesn’t have time to act on an insight, it might as well not exist, and decisions that affect business outcomes get delayed or missed.

The businesses making faster, more defensible workforce decisions aren’t necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated analytics. They’re the ones that understand insight only matters if it shows up inside the systems people already use, like payroll, scheduling and time tracking.

When a scheduling conflict or compliance risk appears in a tool a manager uses every day, they can act on it immediately. When it appears somewhere else, they have to go looking for it, and most small business leaders don’t have that time.

This is where AI has the potential to change the equation. The most effective AI tools do more than generate reports or highlight trends. They proactively surface relevant insights, offer recommendations and deliver guidance within the workflows where managers already spend their time. AI is most valuable when it shortens the distance between knowing and doing, while giving people the context they need to apply their own judgment.

Small business leaders aren’t struggling because they lack workforce data. They’re struggling because valuable insights are often separated from the systems where workforce decisions actually happen. Closing that gap means being more deliberate about which data matters, where it needs to appear and who has the authority to act on it. It doesn’t mean simply adding another AI tool to the tech stack.

Start by auditing where your team’s data lives compared with where decisions actually get made. If those are two different places, that’s the first gap to close. Then look at how much of your workforce data requires a separate login or report to access. Every extra step is another chance for useful information to lose its relevance before it can inform a good decision.

Next, decide where AI can provide meaningful support without removing human judgment from the process. The goal isn’t to automate every workforce decision. It’s to give the right person the right information, in the right context, at the moment it’s most useful.

What separates the businesses that get this right has less to do with how much they invest in AI and more to do with whether workforce insight is built into the flow of daily work. As small business leaders face growing pressure to explain decisions in real time, speed, context and accountability are becoming real competitive advantages.

The next chapter of AI won’t be defined by how much information it can generate. It will be defined by how well it helps leaders make smarter, more timely decisions. Businesses that can move from insight to action faster, without sacrificing human judgment, will be better positioned to adapt to change, support their workforce and compete in an increasingly complex environment.

Small business owners have access to more workforce data than ever, and that data may hold insights hiding in plain sight. Most business leaders can track turnover, overtime, engagement, cost per hire and more on real-time dashboards. What they really need is the ability to turn that data into a decision before the moment that matters has passed.

That gap was highlighted in Paychex’s 2026 Business Leaders Priorities Report, which found that AI adoption and usage rank among the top challenges keeping businesses tied to slower, costlier processes. Many people assume the barrier is a lack of information. In reality, most small businesses already have plenty of workforce data and plenty of tools telling them what it means. The real barrier is speed and, increasingly, proof.

HR leaders are now expected to justify workforce decisions to the C-suite as they happen, not just at the end of a quarter. Decisions are often made before a meeting ends. Leaders need a clear view of their workforce, including why a staffing or scheduling decision was made, before the change shows up on a P&L.

#5451. Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal

Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though.

The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though.

Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the options themselves. Those notional figures can make positions look far larger than the sums actually invested, while revealing little about the firm’s overall exposure once offsetting trades are taken into account. A large reported position, in other words, is not necessarily a huge directional bet.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after more than three decades at the helm of the company he cofounded in 1993. In his place, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang’s departure comes days after bombshell media reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former exec at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence authorities suspect of working for Beijing.

In a message to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized. He also said he supported an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The bad news didn’t stop there for Huang, though. Just three days later, the New York Times reported that the 63-year-old also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that he had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, as well.

Reuters reported in August, citing a person familiar, that Jane Street had so far generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue in 2026. That surpassed its $39.6 billion total for all of 2025 and comfortably beat trading revenues for the nation’s largest banks.

Still, there have been some signs of cracks. That same Reuters report over the summer said Jane Street took a $15 billion hit, partly from its exposure to AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness. Situational Awareness, started by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, sold the bulk of its equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after the market downturn triggered margin calls. Jane Street told employees that the drawdown had left its investment roughly flat for the year, though it remained profitable over the full period, per Reuters. Jane Street has not confirmed this report.

Morgan Chittum is a reporter at Fortune covering finance.

#5450. Your Customers Are Asking AI About Your Company. Here’s How to Audit What It Says.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is changing how customers research businesses. CEOs need this eight-step, modern reputation audit to figure out what customers are seeing.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result.

They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website.

That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing.

Google reported this year that AI Overviews had more than 2.5 billion monthly active users and AI Mode had surpassed 1 billion monthly users. CEOs should account for this behavior in the same way they learned to pay attention to Google results and online reviews.

I work in online reputation management, and at my company Reputation Pros, we recommend treating a reputation audit as a recurring business process. You do not need sophisticated software to start. You just need the right questions and a system for recording what you find. Here is an audit I recommend.

Typing your company name into an AI platform will not tell you enough. Instead, put yourself in the position of a prospective customer conducting due diligence. Ask questions that require the platform to explain what it knows about your company.

Start by copying and customizing this prompt: “I’m considering doing business with [COMPANY NAME]. Research its online reputation as a prospective customer would. Summarize what the company is known for, common positive themes, recurring complaints or criticisms, significant controversies and information that could reasonably affect a customer’s decision. Separate verified facts from allegations or opinions. Where possible, identify the sources supporting each important claim and flag information that may be outdated or uncertain.”

Run the same prompt through several major AI platforms. Do not focus solely on whether the answers sound positive or negative. Look for patterns.

Does the same complaint appear several times? Does one platform emphasize an old controversy? Does another describe your company incorrectly? Which publications, review sites or other sources appear repeatedly?

Record the results. One response does not define your reputation. Differences between platforms can show you where additional investigation is necessary.

CEOs naturally focus on branded searches, but customers do not always begin there. Someone looking for a financial adviser, attorney, software company or home services provider may start by asking for reputable companies in a particular market. The customer may then compare two or three businesses before searching any company individually.

Test that part of the journey too. Use questions such as:

Pay attention to how your company appears in those answers. Do not assume that an omission means something is wrong. Instead, investigate whether credible online sources clearly establish the expertise, history and services your company claims.

This exercise can reveal a problem that a branded Google search will miss: The information people find about your company may look fine, while the broader information environment barely associates your company with the category you want to lead.

Customers are not the only people conducting online research. Potential employees, investors, vendors and business partners can investigate company leadership before making decisions. A CEO’s online reputation deserves its own audit.

Try this: “Research [CEO’S NAME] as if you were a potential business partner conducting due diligence. Summarize their professional background, current business affiliations, documented accomplishments, controversies, lawsuits or regulatory matters and recurring criticism. Distinguish verified facts from allegations and opinions. Identify the sources supporting significant claims and flag information that appears outdated, conflicting or uncertain.”

Check the basic facts first. Is the current position correct? Are former positions described as current? Are business affiliations accurate? Does the answer confuse the CEO with someone who has a similar name?

Do not ignore an error because it happens to make the CEO look good. An inaccurate award, inflated job title or incorrect company affiliation can create credibility problems just as easily as negative misinformation.

Executives sometimes see an unfavorable result and immediately ask how to remove it. Ask whether it is accurate first.

I use five simple classifications when examining reputation issues:

Those categories force you to distinguish between information that damages your reputation and information that you simply dislike.

A legitimate negative customer review requires a different response from a false claim about your company. An accurate article from six years ago requires a different approach from a biography that incorrectly lists an executive’s former employer.

AI can help organize this part of the audit. Copy a concerning response and ask: “Extract every factual claim in the following response that can be independently verified. Organize the claims by Claim, Source Cited, Verification Needed and Potential Business Impact. Do not assume a claim is accurate because it appears in the response.”

Then verify the important claims yourself using reliable sources. Do not use one AI system to declare another AI system correct. Use AI to identify what needs checking. Use primary and authoritative sources to determine what is true.

An unfavorable AI answer is often the symptom rather than the underlying problem. Investigate the sources behind it.

You may discover an outdated executive biography, an old news article, incorrect directory information, inconsistent company descriptions or customer complaints appearing across multiple sites. Ask the AI platform to show its work when the product supports citations. You can also use this prompt: “Based only on the sources available in your answer, identify the sources that support the major claims about [COMPANY]. For each source, list the claim it supports, its publication date if available and whether newer authoritative information appears to conflict with it. Do not infer a source if you cannot identify one.”

Then open the sources. I consider this one of the most important steps in a modern reputation audit. Asking “How do we change this AI answer?” too early can send a company in the wrong direction.

Ask a better question: “Why does this information exist?” A factual problem at the source gives you something concrete to investigate.

AI has expanded reputation management, but it has not completely replaced traditional search yet.

Search your company name, executive names and relevant combinations such as your company plus “reviews,” “complaints,” “lawsuit” and other terms a prospective customer might reasonably use.

Look beyond position. A negative article does not become significant simply because it ranks highly. Determine its date, source, context and accuracy. Find out whether multiple independent sources support the underlying claim or whether dozens of pages repeat information originating from a single source.

The same principle applies to positive coverage. Ten websites repeating the same press release do not provide the same independent validation as 10 separate authoritative sources.

Your audit should measure the quality of the information surrounding your company, not simply count positive and negative links.

Review management creates another risk CEOs should examine. The Federal Trade Commission’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. It addresses practices including fake or false reviews and incentives conditioned on a review expressing a particular positive or negative sentiment.

The FTC sent warning letters to 10 companies in December 2025 over potential violations of the rule and noted that violations can result in substantial civil penalties. Ask your marketing and customer service teams how they request reviews.

Are incentives involved? Does anyone ask specifically for a five-star review? Do employees write reviews? Does an outside vendor manage the process? Does anyone discourage dissatisfied customers from leaving legitimate feedback?

CEOs should understand the answers. I recommend one simple test: Could you comfortably explain your review-generation process to a regulator? If you hesitate, investigate it.

Finish the audit by creating a basic spreadsheet. You only need seven columns:

Run the same core questions every quarter and compare the findings.

Label accurate information and isolated criticism as issues to monitor. Investigate recurring inconsistencies, outdated information and unsupported claims. Prioritize consequential factual errors, impersonation and rapidly spreading false information for action.

Consistency matters more than complexity. The first audit tells you what your reputation looks like today. Repeating the process shows you where it is moving.

A company preparing for an acquisition, leadership change, product launch or other major event may need to run the audit more frequently. Most CEOs can start with a quarterly review and adjust based on the risks they uncover.

Your goal is not to make every search result positive or force every AI platform to praise your company. Neither goal is realistic. Your goal is to know what customers can discover about you, understand where that information comes from and correct factual problems where you legitimately can.

In 2026, people increasingly ask machines to help them evaluate businesses and the people running them. CEOs should know what those machines are finding before an important customer, employee or business partner asks.

Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result.

They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website.

That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing.

#5449. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.
